# INTRODUCTION

AUTHOR: Emma Berninger

DATE: 11/13/2026

PURPOSE: *This file goes through the process of fitting and selecting a 'best' model for the data.*

*This dataset includes many variables relating to the Melbourne housing market. The data was scraped from the publicly available records of the Australian real estate website **Domain**.*

# PART ONE: READING DATA AND PREPROCESSING

## READING DATA

*Bringing necessary packages into current session.*

```{r}
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(bundle)
```

*Reading in the original data.*

```{r}
housing_data <- read_csv('MELBOURNE_HOUSE_PRICES_LESS.csv')

#Checking structure of dataset to see the types of variables
str(housing_data)
```

## PREPROCESSING

*Checking to see if there are any NAs.*

```{r}
colSums(is.na(housing_data))
#Some NAs in Price variable, will be removed later on!
```

*Checking unique values of categorical variables (**Postcode** is included in this, although it was read in as a numeric variable).*

```{r}
unique(housing_data$Suburb)
unique(housing_data$Address)
unique(housing_data$Type)
unique(housing_data$Method)
unique(housing_data$SellerG)
unique(housing_data$Date)
unique(housing_data$Postcode)
unique(housing_data$Regionname)
unique(housing_data$CouncilArea)
#Some of these variables have too many unique values to be useful for analysis. I will be removing the Suburb, Address, SellerG, Date, and Postcode variables.
```

*Based on what I learned from the **str()** function and the EDA, I am going to change the categorical variables into factors, remove any variables that have too many unique values to be analyzed, and remove the NAs in the **Price*** *variable.*

```{r}
#Changing categorical variables into factors
housing_data <- housing_data |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(Type, Method, Regionname, CouncilArea),
      as.factor
    )
  )

str(housing_data)
```

*Removing variables with too many unique values to be used in analysis.*

```{r}
housing_data <- housing_data |>
  subset(select = -c(Suburb, Address, SellerG, Date, Postcode))

str(housing_data)
```

*Removing NAs in **Price** variable.*

```{r}
clean_data <- subset(housing_data, !is.na(Price))

#Checking NAs again
colSums(is.na(clean_data))
#No NAs!
```

*Saving the full dataset for later use*.

```{r}
save(clean_data, file = 'clean_data.RData')
```

# PART TWO: SPLITTING DATA AND MAKING MODELS

## SPLITTING DATA

```{r}
#Setting seed to make things reproducible
set.seed(63023)

#Splitting data
housing_split <- initial_split(clean_data, prop = 0.70)

#Checking split
housing_split

#Naming split data
housing_test <- testing(housing_split)
housing_train <- training(housing_split)
```

## CREATING & FITTING MODELS

*The response that I would like to analyze is the **Price** variable.*

*Creating 5 cross-validation folds.*

```{r}
housing_folds <- vfold_cv(housing_train, v = 5)
housing_folds
```

*Creating recipe for the model workflow.*

```{r}
#Turning factors into dummy variables, everything else stays the same
recipe_1 <- recipe(
  Price ~.,
  data = housing_train
) |>
  step_dummy(Type, Method, Regionname, CouncilArea)

recipe_1
```

### REGRESSION TREE

*A **Regression Tree** is a method of prediction that splits a predictor space into multiple regions. You can make a different prediction in each region. **Regression Trees** are specifically used to predict a **continuous response variable**, with the **mean of observations** within each region as the prediction.*

*For this method, I'm choosing **RMSE** as the metric. This is because it will measure the amount of error there is between the true observed values and the predicted values. This makes it a reliable way of measuring how well fit our model is.*

```{r}
#Creating model for workflow
tree_model <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune()
) |>
  set_engine('rpart') |>
  set_mode('regression')

#Putting together workflow
tree_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe_1) |>
  add_model(tree_model)

#Making a tuning grid
tree_grid <- tree_workflow |>
  tune_grid(
    resamples = housing_folds,
    grid = grid_regular(
      cost_complexity(),
      tree_depth(),
      levels = 3
    )
  )

#Finding best metric value
best_metrics <- tree_grid |>
  select_best(metric = 'rmse')

best_metrics

#Finalizing workflow
tree_final <- tree_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(best_metrics)

#Fitting model with training data
tree_fit <- tree_final |>
  fit(housing_train)
```

### RANDOM FOREST

*A **Random Forest** is an ensemble tree method of prediction. It creates multiple trees using **bootstrap aggregation** and averages the results across all trees. This method uses a random group of predictors to analyze each tree, as opposed to using all predictors at each step, which is what the relatively similar **Bagged Tree** method does. This method is similar to the **Regression Tree*** *model in the sense that they both use a branching technique to analyze their data, but **Random Forests** are different due to the fact that they are ensemble trees, meaning that there are multiple trees.*

*I am also using **RMSE** as the metric for this model. The reason for this is the same as when I used this metric for the **Regression Tree**. I believe that the **RMSE** is a good general metric for most models.*

```{r}
#Creating model for workflow
forest_model <- rand_forest(
  mtry = tune(),
  min_n = tune(),
  trees = 500
) |>
  set_engine('ranger', importance = 'impurity') |>
  set_mode('regression')

#Putting together workflow
forest_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe_1) |>
  add_model(forest_model)

#Making a tuning grid
forest_grid <- forest_workflow |>
  tune_grid(
    resamples = housing_folds,
    grid = grid_regular(
      mtry(range = c(2, 7)),
      min_n(range = c(2, 7)),
      levels = 3
    )
  )

#Finding best metric value
best_metrics <- forest_grid |>
  select_best(metric = 'rmse')

best_metrics

#Finalizing workflow
forest_final <- forest_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(best_metrics)

#Fitting model with training data
forest_fit <- forest_final |>
  fit(housing_train)
```

*Comparing models and finding the best fit*

```{r}
#Using last_fit to fit regression tree model to entire training set and comparing with test set
last_tree <- last_fit(
  tree_final,
  housing_split,
  metrics = metric_set(
    yardstick::rmse
  )
)

#Using last_fit to fit random forest model to entire training set and comparing with test set
last_forest <- last_fit(
  forest_final,
  housing_split,
  metrics = metric_set(
    yardstick::rmse
  )
)

#Putting results in a tibble
last_fit_results <- bind_rows(
  collect_metrics(last_tree) |>
    mutate(model = 'Regression Tree'),
  
  collect_metrics(last_forest) |>
    mutate(model = 'Random Forest')
)

last_fit_results
```

*Our best model is the **Regression Tree** model! It has an RMSE of 313118.5, while the **Random Forest** model has an RMSE of 355015.0. We will use our **Regression Tree** model to fit our full data set.*

*Saving the **tree_final** model for later use.*

```{r}
save(tree_final, file = 'tree_final.RData')
```

*Fitting the best model to the full data set*

```{r}
full_fit <- tree_final |>
  fit(clean_data)

full_fit
```
